Microsoft's Dynamics 365 revenues also increased 13% year over year in the fourth quarter, showing continued demand for its business applications.
Oracle is taking a similar approach by adding AI capabilities to its cloud applications. The company is moving beyond traditional per-seat licensing to consumption-based token bundles. This approach lets enterprises pre-purchase agentic AI capacity in a predictable, scalable way across application tiers.
In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Oracle's Cloud Applications revenues reached $4.1 billion, up 10% year over year, while total cloud revenues jumped 47% to $9.9 billion. Oracle's AI-focused cloud strategy is also driving strong demand across its broader platform.

Salesforce vs. UiPath: Which AI Automation Stock Gives Investors More for Their Money?
UiPath costs about $13 a share. Salesforce costs more than $230. Investors looking for affordable exposure to enterprise AI could easily reach for the wrong shortcut: the smaller share price says nothing about how much cash-generating power they are buying.
Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) and UiPath, Inc. (NYSE:PATH) approach automation from different starting points. Salesforce can sell agents into its existing customer-management software base. UiPath wants to coordinate work across applications, combining AI agents with the more predictable automation businesses already use. Both can benefit if companies move from experimenting with AI to paying for completed work. The question is how much execution investors must assume at today's prices.
Snowflake generated positive free cash flow, yet its stock-compensation bill was much larger. Our analysis asks what remains for owners when that bill enters the valuation.
Salesforce vs. UiPath: Which AI Automation Stock Gives Investors More for Their Money?
Six stocks ranked above UiPath when growth, cash generation and valuation were weighed together in our 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy Under $25. The names above it offer a useful test of what an investor gives up by choosing automation.
The smaller company carries the higher cash-flow multiple
At the October 2 close, Salesforce traded at approximately 12.8 times trailing free cash flow, compared with 18.8 times for UiPath. Those calculations divide equity market value by operating cash flow less capital expenditures, avoiding a comparison between differently adjusted profit figures. Salesforce generated about $15.15 billion on that basis over the trailing year; UiPath generated roughly $363 million.
The gap gives Salesforce a stronger starting position for investors who want established cash production. It does not settle the comparison. Salesforce also carries substantial debt, while UiPath reported $1.405 billion of cash and marketable securities at July 31. UiPath has more financial flexibility relative to its size. Its higher equity cash-flow multiple partly reflects that balance-sheet difference.
Neither cash-flow figure deducts stock compensation as a cash expense. Buybacks can reduce the resulting dilution, but consume money that would otherwise belong to shareholders.
Insider Monkey's hedge fund database counted 99 Salesforce holders in Q2 2026 (June 30), down from 101 in Q1 2026 (March 31), while UiPath rose from 40 to 48. Harris Associates increased its Salesforce position approximately 8.3% to 16.15 million shares. Rima Senvest increased its UiPath holding about 55.2% to 12.09 million shares. Those are completed-quarter positions, not evidence of what the managers are buying today.
Salesforce's August 26 results for the July quarter showed $11.345 billion of revenue, up 11%, including $456 million from Informatica. That acquired contribution matters: the reported growth rate cannot all be credited to AI adoption. Still, a 20.5% GAAP operating margin shows an established business already earning substantial operating profit while funding its expansion.
UiPath reported on September 3 that July-quarter revenue grew 13% to $410.3 million. More revealing was its 109% dollar-based net retention rate: existing customers expanded their annualized business, but not at a pace that makes rapid acceleration inevitable. Its annualized renewal run-rate grew 12%, and management guided full-year revenue to roughly $1.79 billion.
UiPath's opportunity is to become the control layer companies need when agents must interact with software, follow rules and hand work to people. That could make its independence valuable across mixed technology environments. The risk is that application vendors and model providers absorb enough automation into their own products to make a separate orchestration bill harder to justify.
Salesforce faces a related problem from the other side. Its distribution is valuable only if customers pay for the new capabilities. AI could also change how customers buy software, putting pressure on traditional pricing. A lower cash-flow multiple offers some compensation for that uncertainty, but cannot protect investors from a sustained deterioration in the underlying business.
A preference, with a clear reason to change it
The September 15 short-interest snapshot was much heavier for UiPath: approximately 104.2 million shares, or 25.8% of float, compared with Salesforce's 32.35 million shares, or about 4.1%. That can amplify volatility without deciding which business will win.
Salesforce gets the preference for investors seeking cash generation at a restrained price. UiPath is the more demanding bet on independent orchestration. Sustained improvement in customer expansion, accompanied by faster cash growth per share, would justify revisiting that choice. A $13 stock does not need to become a software giant to work, but it does need to earn the premium investors already pay for its cash flow.
While we acknowledge the potential of CRM and PATH as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Salesforce: Steady Revenue Generation at Large Scale
Salesforce (CRM -0.84%) primarily generates revenue by providing cloud-based customer relationship management (CRM) platforms and enterprise software to global businesses.
During the most recent quarter, it finalized its strategic acquisition of customer agent platform Fin to actively integrate specialized technical teams to capitalize on the artificial intelligence boom.

CrowdStrike: Delivering Faster Revenue Expansion
CrowdStrike (CRWD +1.48%) primarily generates revenue through subscription sales of its cloud-native cybersecurity platforms and endpoint protection modules to enterprises.
It recently appointed a new Chief Product Officer to oversee ongoing platform development initiatives, while it concurrently expanded a major strategic partnership with Schwarz Digits to offer localized sovereign cloud security capabilities specifically tailored for large European enterprise clients.

That said, CrowdStrike is enjoying quarter-over-quarter sales growth, which is much faster than the year-over-year increases typically seen with successful companies. This speaks to the strong demand it's seeing as a result of AI's arrival.
Artificial intelligence is able to hack into an organization with unprecedented speed and skill. This has created a tailwind for CrowdStrike's business, as the need for cybersecurity resilient to AI attacks has risen in importance. In a sign of the strong demand the company is seeing, the $1.5 billion in revenue in its fiscal Q2, ended July 31, represented outstanding 26% year-over-year growth.
That's not to say Salesforce's business is not doing well, since it continues to enjoy consistent year-over-year sales increases. The revenue of $11.3 billion in its fiscal Q2 was an 11% jump over the prior year. Still, that pales in comparison to CrowdStrike's rapid revenue acceleration.

UiPath costs about $13 a share. Salesforce costs more than $230. Investors looking for affordable exposure to enterprise AI could easily reach for the wrong shortcut: the smaller share price says nothing about how much cash-generating power they are buying.
Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) and UiPath, Inc. (NYSE:PATH) approach automation from different starting points. Salesforce can sell agents into its existing customer-management software base. UiPath wants to coordinate work across applications, combining AI agents with the more predictable automation businesses already use. Both can benefit if companies move from experimenting with AI to paying for completed work. The question is how much execution investors must assume at today’s prices.
Snowflake generated positive free cash flow, yet its stock-compensation bill was much larger. Our analysis asks what remains for owners when that bill enters the valuation.
Six stocks ranked above UiPath when growth, cash generation and valuation were weighed together in our 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy Under $25. The names above it offer a useful test of what an investor gives up by choosing automation.
The smaller company carries the higher cash-flow multiple
At the October 2 close, Salesforce traded at approximately 12.8 times trailing free cash flow, compared with 18.8 times for UiPath. Those calculations divide equity market value by operating cash flow less capital expenditures, avoiding a comparison between differently adjusted profit figures. Salesforce generated about $15.15 billion on that basis over the trailing year; UiPath generated roughly $363 million.
The gap gives Salesforce a stronger starting position for investors who want established cash production. It does not settle the comparison. Salesforce also carries substantial debt, while UiPath reported $1.405 billion of cash and marketable securities at July 31. UiPath has more financial flexibility relative to its size. Its higher equity cash-flow multiple partly reflects that balance-sheet difference.
Neither cash-flow figure deducts stock compensation as a cash expense. Buybacks can reduce the resulting dilution, but consume money that would otherwise belong to shareholders.
Insider Monkey’s hedge fund database counted 99 Salesforce holders in Q2 2026 (June 30), down from 101 in Q1 2026 (March 31), while UiPath rose from 40 to 48. Harris Associates increased its Salesforce position approximately 8.3% to 16.15 million shares. Rima Senvest increased its UiPath holding about 55.2% to 12.09 million shares. Those are completed-quarter positions, not evidence of what the managers are buying today.
Salesforce’s August 26 results for the July quarter showed $11.345 billion of revenue, up 11%, including $456 million from Informatica. That acquired contribution matters: the reported growth rate cannot all be credited to AI adoption. Still, a 20.5% GAAP operating margin shows an established business already earning substantial operating profit while funding its expansion.
UiPath reported on September 3 that July-quarter revenue grew 13% to $410.3 million. More revealing was its 109% dollar-based net retention rate: existing customers expanded their annualized business, but not at a pace that makes rapid acceleration inevitable. Its annualized renewal run-rate grew 12%, and management guided full-year revenue to roughly $1.79 billion.
UiPath’s opportunity is to become the control layer companies need when agents must interact with software, follow rules and hand work to people. That could make its independence valuable across mixed technology environments. The risk is that application vendors and model providers absorb enough automation into their own products to make a separate orchestration bill harder to justify.
Salesforce faces a related problem from the other side. Its distribution is valuable only if customers pay for the new capabilities. AI could also change how customers buy software, putting pressure on traditional pricing. A lower cash-flow multiple offers some compensation for that uncertainty, but cannot protect investors from a sustained deterioration in the underlying business.
A preference, with a clear reason to change it
The September 15 short-interest snapshot was much heavier for UiPath: approximately 104.2 million shares, or 25.8% of float, compared with Salesforce’s 32.35 million shares, or about 4.1%. That can amplify volatility without deciding which business will win.
Salesforce gets the preference for investors seeking cash generation at a restrained price. UiPath is the more demanding bet on independent orchestration. Sustained improvement in customer expansion, accompanied by faster cash growth per share, would justify revisiting that choice. A $13 stock does not need to become a software giant to work, but it does need to earn the premium investors already pay for its cash flow.

Salesforce, the #1 AI CRM, today announced it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Listen Labs, an AI-powered customer research and human simulation platform. Listen Labs’s AI agents design studies, conduct in-depth research, and synthesize insights, automating the lifecycle of connecting with customers and analyzing their feedback. Listen Labs streamlines this process from months to days, helping turn qualitative feedback into actionable insights for decision-makers and context for agents at scale.
The acquisition will expand Salesforce’s customer and user understanding capabilities, complementing Marketing Cloud, Service Cloud, and our broader AI portfolio. With Listen Labs, Salesforce will empower companies worldwide to move beyond static surveys and traditional market research to understand — and even simulate — what customers will do and why, then turn those insights into action.
“Listen Labs has reimagined customer experience, market research, and customer simulation with AI agents that can conduct meaningful research and uncover context behind customer and user feedback,” said Aman Naimat, President of AI Labs, Salesforce. “We look forward to expanding access to these agentic capabilities through Salesforce, helping more companies and governments make faster, better-informed decisions that deliver exceptional customer experiences.”
“Companies have always wanted to hear from every customer, but until now it was only possible to talk to a handful,” said Alfred Wahlforss, CEO and Co-Founder of Listen Labs. “With AI, a company can now have thousands of real conversations at once and even simulate how customers will respond before making a move. Together with Salesforce, we’ll put that understanding at the heart of every decision.”
Listen Labs helps companies move from research questions to customer insights in days instead of months. Its AI agents autonomously design studies, intelligently recruit participants, conduct in-depth research, and synthesize the findings in a single platform. Agents can draw from a global network of more than 50 million participants and run interviews around the clock in more than 120 languages, gathering perspectives from more people and markets in less time.
Decision-makers can also explore how customers might respond to a new product, marketing message, or idea before bringing it to market. Listen Labs’s digital twins, AI simulations grounded in real customer behavior, generate simulated responses that help teams and agents compare approaches and refine their plans before further customer or user testing.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of Salesforce’s fiscal year 2027, subject to satisfaction of customary closing conditions, including the receipt of required regulatory clearance.

Salesforce launches Hyperagent in Slack for autonomous AI deployment
The $27.7 billion Slack acquisition finally gets its full AI payoff as Salesforce turns its workplace chat app into a command center for autonomous agents.
Salesforce is rolling out Hyperagent capabilities inside Slack, enabling teams to deploy autonomous AI agents that can source leads, generate reports, update CRM records, and execute multi-step workflows without leaving the chat interface.
The move represents the most aggressive integration yet between Salesforce’s Agentforce AI platform and the workplace messaging tool it acquired for $27.7 billion back in 2021.
The core of this launch is a redesigned Slackbot that has been rebuilt from the ground up as a functional AI agent. The new one can pull prospect lists, run complex Salesforce reports, and update records across your CRM, all triggered by natural language commands in a Slack channel.
Agents built in Salesforce’s Agent Builder tool can be deployed directly into Slack workspaces, where they inherit permissions from both platforms.
The upgraded Slackbot became generally available to Business+ and Enterprise+ customers starting in January 2026. According to Salesforce, around 80,000 internal testers used the product before launch, making it the fastest adopted product in the company’s history.

Meet the new hires: Hunter, Paige, and friends
Salesforce introduced specialized “job-ready” agents tailored for specific operational functions. Hunter is designed for sales teams, handling lead sourcing and pipeline management. Paige covers IT and HR workflows. These agents were introduced in September 2026 as part of a broader Agentforce expansion.
A sales rep can tag Hunter in a Slack channel and ask it to find companies matching a specific profile, pull their contact information from the CRM, and draft outreach sequences. An IT manager can ask Paige to check the status of open tickets or route a support request.
The bigger picture: AI agents as infrastructure
Slack has more than 200,000 paid customers globally. Embedding AI agents directly into those existing workflows eliminates the adoption friction that kills most enterprise AI projects.
Microsoft has been pursuing a similar strategy with Copilot agents inside Teams, and Google is building agent capabilities into Workspace.
Agentforce agents can read and write to Salesforce’s CRM while communicating with teams in real time through Slack. The dual-permission model means agents inherit permissions from both Slack and Salesforce, addressing enterprise security concerns.

Salesforce Is Cheap. ServiceNow Is Growing Faster. Here’s the Stock I’d Buy.
Two AI software giants both reported strong agentic bookings this summer, but they sit at opposite ends of the valuation spectrum. The case for buying the cheaper one is stronger than it looks, and the case against it is equally…
Published September 28, 2026, 1:30pm ET · 3 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Dynamic market data and urban skylines reflect the complex landscape income investors navigate when comparing financial institutions like Bank of America and U.S. Bancorp for dividend opportunities. © Pixels Hunter / Shutterstock.com
ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW | NOW Price Prediction) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) both reported this summer with the same message: agentic AI is now showing up in bookings. They differ sharply on price.
ServiceNow grew revenue 24% and trades at 27x forward earnings. Salesforce grew 10.8% at about 14x. So investors have to pick between speed and value.
Governance Sells at ServiceNow While Salesforce Customers Keep Refilling the Tank
ServiceNow’s subscription revenue reached $3.877B, up 24.5%. That is rare speed at this scale. Its AI annual contract value (ACV) passed $1B. More than 500 customers went live on AI Control Tower within six months.
That product manages AI agents across other vendors’ platforms, which puts ServiceNow in charge of everyone else’s AI. The CFO summed up the pitch: “Customers aren’t paying us for tokens, they’re paying for resolutions.” ServiceNow is also moving onto Salesforce’s territory.
Salesforce’s current remaining performance obligations (cRPO, or contracted revenue due within 12 months) rose 14%, up from 13% last quarter. The backlog is starting to speed up again. Agentforce annual recurring revenue exceeded $1.5B, and 50% of bookings came from customers buying more credits. That points to real usage beyond pilot projects.
I remain skeptical of the headline earnings, though. Non-GAAP EPS of $5.90 included about $2.53/share from investment profits. The Informatica acquisition also added $456M in revenue.
One Wants to Govern Every Agent. One Wants to Own the Customer Record.
ServiceNow is buying its way into security. Its chief executive called cybersecurity “a massive tailwind”. The acquisitions carry a cost: GAAP subscription gross margin slipped to 73.5% from 80% because of amortization of acquired assets.
Salesforce leans on upselling and buybacks. Only 5% of sales and service users have upgraded to premium editions, which carry a 60% to 80% price premium. That leaves plenty of room to upsell. Its $25B accelerated buyback cut diluted shares to 821M from 962M.
ServiceNow’s steeper fall has already narrowed its premium. It still costs about twice as much per dollar of forward earnings.
Q3 Reveals Whether ServiceNow’s Federal Pull-Forward Leaves a Gap
ServiceNow guided Q3 subscription growth to about 20.5%, partly because some U.S. federal revenue landed in Q2 instead of Q3. A key question is whether cRPO holds near the 20% guide.
Salesforce’s management expects organic growth to pick up in the second half. Dreamforce landed as a small success even as the stock fell, so investors want proof.
Why I Lean Toward Salesforce at 14 Times Earnings
I think ServiceNow has the better business. Its products are growing faster, and AI Control Tower gives it an unusual position. Still, I lean toward Salesforce at this valuation. A 7.34% free cash flow yield, a growing backlog and a shrinking share count give me several ways to make money.
Growth investors comfortable paying up will prefer ServiceNow. I would change my view if Salesforce’s organic growth stalls in Q3, or if ServiceNow shows the federal shift left no gap.

10 Salesforce Solution Providers Reshaping CRM In The AI Era
OSF Digital, Accenture, IBM Consulting, Rosetree Solutions and Cognizant are among the list makers.
Agentforce and other investments by Salesforce into artificial intelligence and agentic AI means that solution providers who can push beyond the vendor’s classic customer relationship management business are the ones most likely to win in this new workforce technology era.
From some of the largest multinational global system integrators with tens of thousands of Salesforce certifications to smaller, more specialized boutique partners, some of the biggest standout solution providers partnered with San Francisco-based Salesforce were on display during the vendor’s Dreamforce 2026 conference.
With solutions spanning industry expertise, these solution providers were some of the most impressive to CRN based on their Dreamforce 2026 presence and the Salesforce solutions they are bringing to market.
Some of these partners have also landed admittance into new partner opportunities Salesforce has introduced, including the Forward Deployed Engineering Partner Network, and landed Partner of the Year Awards for Salesforce’s 2027 fiscal year.
[RELATED: 5 Biggest Channel Takeaways From Salesforce Dreamforce 2026]
Sean Catlin, executive vice president and global head of strategy at Québec-based Salesforce solution provider OSF Digital, one of the list makers, told CRN in an interview that the company has been seeing demand for its proof of value (POV) applied AI use case identification capabilities, which helps customers identify the areas of their business that are most likely to deliver returns on AI investments.
“You have to get the customer to be comfortable with being uncomfortable first,” Catlin said.
Other Salesforce partners to make the list include:
Read on for some of the most impressive solution providers in the Salesforce ecosystem who are taking CRM and SaaS into the agentic future.
IBM’s close relationship with Salesforce extends beyond product integrations, with IBM Consulting distinguishing itself through Agentforce deployments, AI accelerators and deep Salesforce expertise.
IBM Consulting—No. 8 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500—is a Salesforce Partner of the Year for the 2027 fiscal year—for its work deploying Agentforce-powered autonomous agents that make decisions and execute actions across business workflows for Nestle.
The consulting division has accelerators for all 19 Salesforce Industry clouds and leverages the IBM Consulting Advantage AI services platform, library of assistants and IBM Garage collaborative delivery framework, according to IBM. IBM Consulting has helped Salesforce users unify data foundations, streamline agent architecture, orchestrate enterprise resource planning (ERP) transformations and more.
On the product side, IBM’s deep partnership with Salesforce extends to 22,700-plus Salesforce certifications held by IBM employees and more than 150 prebuilt assets, assessments, quick-starts and accelerators designed to enhance native Salesforce functionality and get products and services in-market faster.
Users of the Armonk, N.Y.-based mainframe giant’s Z products and Salesforce’s Data 360 can enable AI agents to access mainframe and enterprise data in real time, with a Zero Copy integration that accelerates insights, reduces data movement costs and enforces governance across hybrid environments, according to IBM.
IBM’s Watsonx Employee Support Agent can bring improved human resources automation into the interface of Salesforce’s Slack communications application. And the IBM Watsonx Sales Prospecting Agent can surface enriched company data, update CRM records and automate outreach and research for sellers, as another example, according to IBM.
The recently released IBM Bob multirole coding collaborator can create the framework for orchestrated enterprise AI, with Slack providing a collaboration layer integrated with Watsonx capabilities and Salesforce customer data in another example.
IBM’s Salesforce-related customers include MOL Group, the Recording Academy nonprofit organization that hosts the Grammys, Camping World, Evident and Ireland’s Health Service Executive (HSE) when the healthcare and social services provider needed a platform for COVID-19 vaccinations, according to IBM.
Accenture, No. 1 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500, has more than 55,000 Salesforce-skilled employees, accounting for more than 78,000 Salesforce certifications and 577,000 badges in the Salesforce Trailhead online learning platform.
The Dublin-based company ranked as one of Salesforce’s 2027 Partner of the Year Award Winners as a global consulting partner. Last year, it closed on its acquisition of another leading Salesforce partner, NeuraFlash, to further bolster its skills with the vendor.
Accenture leverages a Personalized Experiences on Salesforce offer unifying AI, data integration and human expertise with Agentforce, Data Cloud and Einstein. It has helped wealth management firms accelerate onboarding and automate complex processes and others connect Microsoft Teams and Salesforce to keep the CRM updated based on data in Teams, according to Accenture.
The solution provider’s Cyber.AI platform for agentic enterprises works with Salesforce Shield to surface and prioritize major risks while its agentic software development life cycle (SDLC) framework helps scattered Salesforce knowledge get turned into agent-powered intelligence also usable in third-party products like Anthropic’s Claude and SpaceX’s Cursor.
Accenture is among the Salesforce solution providers to get called out for deeper investments in Life Sciences Cloud in April, leading the first client migration in the industry and bringing Agentforce Voice capabilities to clients in pharmaceuticals, medical technology and other sectors, according to Salesforce.
Accenture and NeuraFlash’s Salesforce customers include Workday, FedEx Freight, Novartis, Zayo, Adecco, Synopsys, Taco Bell, Canon and Queensland University of Technology (QUT), according to Accenture.
Slalom, No. 33 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500, received a 2027 Salesforce Partner of the Year for its work as a consulting partner on the Agentforce system of agency.
The Seattle-based solution provider took home the award for its work leveraging Agentforce to help U.K. pet care business Pets at Home reduce inbound case volume by about 30 percent, a decrease from around 1,300 typical daily cases down to 900. Customer satisfaction remained above target, according to Slalom.
Slalom is a founding member of the Agentforce Partner Network and touts its ability to build agentic complaints detection on Agentforce for Financial Services and create patient services platforms on Agentforce for Life Sciences, among other capabilities, according to Slalom.
Slalom has more than 14,000 Salesforce certifications and 1,000-plus customers on the platform, according to the solution provider.
The solution provider offers clients an Agentforce Foundations Accelerator for unlocking insights from data, an AI Value Platform for evaluating AI initiatives and a Salesforce Data Cloud Readiness workshop for optimizing data usage. It is also helping customers unlock new digital experiences enabled by Salesforce’s recent Contentful acquisition.
Slalom was among the solution providers to go all in on Salesforce’s Life Sciences Cloud earlier this year, bringing fixed-fee implementations for commercial, medical and patient services and accelerators for deploying agentic capabilities in field effectiveness, patient access and adherence, and operations, according to Salesforce.
Slalom’s Salesforce customers include Hanna Andersson, Mirum Pharmaceuticals, Avetta and Penn Medicine, according to the solution provider.
Tata Consultancy Services and the Coastal and ListEngage businesses it purchased in October and January, respectively, all took home a 2027 Salesforce Partner of the Year award for their work on the Data 360 system of context.
TCS—No. 2 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500—is a partner in Salesforce’s Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) program, co-creating AI‑led, agentic offerings with the vendor, according to the Mumbai, India-based solution provider.
The solution provider’s Crystallus on Salesforce offer promises clients the ability to accelerate digital transformations with pre-configured industry offerings for customer journeys, operations and more. TCS can help clients with change management, content strategy, managed services, Salesforce Lightning migration, application optimization and other activities.
TCS has more than 10,000 certified professionals with more than 32,000 Salesforce certifications and more than 330 Salesforce customers, according to the solution provider.
Its Salesforce customers include Linde, Vantage Towers, Croma, DuPont, Alcatel-Lucent, Stellantis and Tottenham Hotspur, according to TCS.
Cognizant—No. 7 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500—added a 2027 Salesforce Partner of the Year Award to its trophy case for its work as a consulting partner in transforming and scaling.
The Teaneck, N.J.-based solution provider brings together customer experience (CX) expertise, its Neuro AI platform and orchestration framework and Salesforce Agentforce platform prowess to improve client sales, service and engagement divisions, according to Cognizant.
Cognizant’s Salesforce-related offers include Managed Marketing Campaigns for automating manual marketing processes, the Atlas delivery framework for end-to-end transformations, the Revenue Management Framework for Technology for better outcomes from Salesforce Revenue Cloud and the Mortgage 360 digital hub built on Salesforce for mortgage intermediaries, solicitors and introducers, according to the solution provider.
In April, Salesforce named Cognizant as one of the system integrators the vendor was expanding a partnership with around Life Sciences Cloud, with Cognizant leveraging an AI builder approach to modernize clients from legacy platforms and apply agentic AI across commercial and clinical operations, according to Salesforce.
Cognizant was also among the solution providers named to Salesforce’s Forward Deployed Engineering Partner Network that month as well.
The solution provider’s Salesforce customers include Saint-Gobain Abrasives and Volkswagen Group Ireland, according to Cognizant.
OSF Digital representatives at Dreamforce 2026 showcased agents in production drawn from real deployments across industries.
During Dreamforce, representatives with Quebec-based OSF showcased the solution provider’s capabilities around Agentforce Operations, with OSF among the earliest partners to deploy the internal business operations platform, according to the solution provider.
OSF’s Agentforce Operations offer aims to bring together unstructured input transformation, industry process libraries, implementation playbooks, governance frameworks, training and enablement, intellectual property framework and forward-deployed engineering (FDE) pods.
It was one of 10 global Salesforce partners chosen in the early Salesforce FDE Partner Network cohort, according to OSF.
The solution provider also positions itself as a Headless 360 expert to give humans and agents the same governed foundation for operations, with shared rules and permissions plus an audit trail following work wherever it happens.
In 2025, OSF signed 80-plus new logos and closed more than 40 seven-figure range deals, according to the solution provider. It expanded its business in technology, media and telecommunications (TMT), financial services (FINS), manufacturing and other sectors.
In the first half of 2026, OSF onboarded more than 30 new customers with AI and data bookings more than tripling year on year and multi-cloud, multi-million-dollar agentic enterprise deals represented 25 percent of new engagements.
OSF has more than 2,000 customers worldwide, with clients including Mahou San Miguel, Dr. Marte

Salesforce (CRM) Is Buying Back $50 Billion of Stock. What Does That Say About Growth?
Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) authorized a $50 billion share repurchase program in February 2026, then executed half of it within weeks through the largest accelerated share repurchase in corporate history.
Buying back stock is what companies do when they have more cash than ideas. A commitment that size, from a company whose entire market value is under $200 billion, says something about where management expects the next decade of growth to come from. The answer appears to be nowhere in particular.
READ ALSO: MongoDB (MDB) vs Snowflake (SNOW): Which is a Better Stock to Buy?
Salesforce (CRM) Is Buying Back $50 Billion of Stock. What Does That Say About Growth?
The Cash Machine is Genuinely Extraordinary:
Before the criticism, the defense, because the numbers behind it are remarkable. Salesforce generated $17.73 billion of levered free cash flow over the past twelve months on revenue of $43.94 billion. Most software companies never approach that conversion rate.
Operating margin reached 21.38%, and interest income on the cash pile pushed net margin slightly higher at 21.99%. For a business mocked for a decade for never making money, that is a genuine transformation.
Revenue still grew 10.80% in the most recent quarter, and earnings grew 86.90%. With that much cash and a share price that has gone nowhere, buying stock is not obviously the wrong call. Salesforce is down 4.51% over twelve months while the S&P 500 rose about 14%.
Management is effectively saying the shares are cheaper than anything it could buy or build. On a forward multiple of 13.99 times, that is not an unreasonable view.
DON'T MISS: What is Yelp's (YELP) Economic Moat, and is it Widening or Narrowing?
What Buybacks Cannot Buy:
The problem is what the spending pattern implies about the next product cycle.
Salesforce built its position by acquiring and integrating: MuleSoft, Tableau, Slack. That strategy needed capital, and it bought growth. Redirecting the money to buybacks ends it.
The timing is the uncomfortable part. Generative AI is rewriting what enterprise software does, and this is the moment when a company normally spends on building rather than on retiring its own shares. The count has already fallen from 997 million to 895.5 million.
There is a structural argument underneath. Salesforce sells seats to sales and service teams. If AI agents handle more of that work, the number of seats a customer needs stops growing, which is the same question hanging over Adobe.
A buyback does nothing about that. It shrinks the denominator so earnings per share rise even if earnings do not.
The balance sheet also carries $42.38 billion of debt against $11.4 billion of cash, so the repurchases are not being funded from a fortress position.
There is an enterprise software company growing faster than Salesforce that is still spending to build rather than to buy back. Check out our 10 Best Stocks to Buy for High Returns in 2026.
The Valuation Case:
Salesforce closed at $234.69 on October 2, down 4.51% over twelve months. Revenue grew 10.80% last quarter, and earnings grew 86.90%.
The growth is sustainable but slowing. Low double-digit revenue growth from a base that size is respectable and repeatable, and nothing suggests a collapse.
On price, the stock is cheap against the market. It trades at 13.99 times next year's estimates while the S&P 500 trades near 19 times, on a better operating margin than most of it.
Compare it with the companies it actually competes against. Oracle grew revenue 29% last quarter on a 35.63% operating margin and trades at 17.76 times forward. ServiceNow grew 24% and trades at 27.78 times. Salesforce is the cheapest of the three at 13.99 times, and also the slowest growing by some distance.
Conclusion:
The cash generation is the best argument for owning this. Converting revenue into $17.73 billion of free cash flow is exceptional. The operating margin has passed 21%, and the shares cost well under the market on next year's estimates. However, a company committing $50 billion to buying its own stock is telling investors something about its ambitions. Salesforce grew by acquiring, but that era appears over, and the AI question about seat counts arrives exactly as the capital goes to retiring shares instead.

Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) was held by 99 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $6.44 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is down from 101 hedge fund holders with a cumulative investment value of around $6.87 billion in the previous quarter.

As the software market shifts toward products driven by artificial intelligence (AI), investors comparing enterprise software names may find themselves choosing between Salesforce (CRM -0.84%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.68%). This comparison looks at which company offers the better balance of value and growth.
Salesforce describes itself as a global leader in customer relationship management (CRM) technology and is now focused on Agentforce, its line of autonomous AI agents. Palantir sells software platforms that governments and companies use to integrate their data and apply AI to daily operations. For investors researching AI stocks to buy, the two companies present very different financial profiles.
Salesforce sells cloud-based software that helps businesses manage customer relationships and sales pipelines. Its annual report for fiscal 2026, which ended on Jan. 31, 2026, lists 83,334 employees and states that the company sells to businesses across almost every industry. On Aug. 26, 2026, Salesforce said annual recurring revenue from Agentforce had passed $1.5 billion. It completed its acquisition of Fin, an AI customer agent company formerly known as Intercom, on Sept. 10, 2026.
In fiscal 2026, revenue reached approximately $41.5 billion, up 9.6% from the prior fiscal year. Net income was nearly $7.5 billion, and net margin rose to 18% from 16.4%. About $1.0 billion in net gains from strategic investments contributed to that improvement, compared with a small net loss on those investments a year earlier.
As of Jan. 31, 2026, Salesforce had about $14.4 billion in total debt and $59.1 billion in shareholder equity, a debt-to-equity ratio of about 0.2x. Its current ratio, which compares current assets with liabilities due within a year, was roughly 0.8x.
The debt picture has changed since then. Salesforce issued about $25 billion in debt in the quarter that ended April 30, 2026, to fund an accelerated share repurchase, and its July 31, 2026, balance sheet shows $39.3 billion in debt against $38.4 billion in equity, a ratio of about 1.0x.
Free cash flow, defined as operating cash flow minus capital expenditures, was about $14.4 billion in fiscal 2026. Stock-based compensation (SBC) equaled roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which is worth noting because SBC is a non-cash expense that is added back in the cash flow statement.
Palantir develops software platforms that help organizations integrate their data and operations, and it sells them to government agencies and commercial customers.
Government customers supplied 54% of its 2025 revenue. Palantir also works with other companies that investors follow as tech stocks, including a collaboration with Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%) announced on Sept. 10, 2026, and a global partnership with Fujitsu (FJTSF +0.97%). Its commercial customer count reached 870 for the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, up 26% from a year earlier.
In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached roughly $4.5 billion, a 56.2% year-over-year increase. Palantir reported net income of about $1.6 billion. Net margin was about 36.3%, up from 16.1% in 2024.
Palantir had no debt outstanding as of Dec. 31, 2025, resulting in a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x. Its current ratio at that date was approximately 7.1x, indicating ample liquid assets to cover short-term liabilities. Free cash flow, calculated the same way as for Salesforce (operating cash flow minus capital expenditures), was about $2.1 billion.
Palantir's own adjusted free cash flow, which adds back employer payroll taxes tied to stock-based compensation, was about $2.3 billion. SBC equaled roughly 32% of operating cash flow.
Salesforce competes with established enterprise software vendors and AI-native start-ups in a market that its annual report calls highly competitive. Salesforce and its Slack unit sued Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) in London's High Court in April 2026, alleging that the tying and bundling of Teams harmed competition.
Microsoft has said the case lacks merit, and the outcome is uncertain. Salesforce must also integrate large acquisitions such as Informatica, which closed in fiscal 2026, and Fin, and it now carries far more debt than it did at the start of the fiscal year. On Sept. 29, 2026, it also agreed to acquire Listen Labs, an AI customer research company, in a deal it expects to close in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.
Palantir's annual report flags a limited number of customers that account for a substantial portion of its revenue, with the top three supplying 16% of 2025 revenue, and a sales cycle it calls long and unpredictable.
The company depends on third-party computing infrastructure. It also warns that news coverage or other outside scrutiny of the company or its leadership could harm its reputation. A shareholder lawsuit that a federal court dismissed in April 2025 was still on appeal as of June 30, 2026.
Salesforce trades at a much lower forward P/E, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, and a much lower P/S ratio, which measures price relative to sales over the past 12 months.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Salesforce looks like the better buy to me, with the caveat that it's a slower-growing and more indebted company than the fiscal 2026 figures above suggest. On Aug. 26, 2026, management guided for revenue growth of 11% to 12% in fiscal 2027, which ends in January 2027.
By its own math, more than a quarter of that growth comes from the Informatica acquisition. Salesforce also borrowed heavily earlier this year to fund its accelerated share repurchase. Its debt has more than doubled since January and roughly equaled shareholder equity at the end of July. The appeal is the price.
A business that turns about a third of its revenue into free cash flow, at a forward P/E in the mid-teens, leaves room for Agentforce to grow slowly without the investment case falling apart.
Palantir is growing far faster. Its revenue nearly doubled in the second quarter, and on Aug. 3, 2026, management raised its full-year outlook. The catch is a forward P/E ratio more than five times Salesforce's, which leaves the stock with little cushion if growth cools.
Growth rates this high are also hard to sustain as a company gets bigger. I'd rather hold Palantir as a small position in a diversified portfolio than pay that premium for a large one. Even so, a company expanding this quickly with no debt has earned a spot on a growth investor's watch list.

Salesforce Expands AI Bundles: Will Higher Adoption Boost ARR?
Salesforce, Inc. CRM is expanding its AI bundles, aiming to make it easier for customers to adopt its growing suite of artificial intelligence (AI) tools. The company is continuously introducing premium bundles that combine new AI capabilities with its existing applications. Earlier in September 2026, it introduced Core, Advanced and Max editions for Agentforce Sales, Service and Industries, bundling AI, Slack, Tableau Next, security and support into a single purchase.
The early results suggest that its bundled approach could help lift recurring revenues. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, it revealed that bookings from Agentforce One Edition and Agentforce for Apps more than doubled sequentially. Salesforce also stated premium Slack upgrades have tripled since Slackbot launched. These trends indicate that customers are moving from AI trials toward broader purchases.
The impact is already visible in Salesforce's AI business. Agentforce ARR (annual recurring revenues) topped $1.5 billion in the second quarter, up more than 240% year over year. Combined Agentforce and Data 360 ARR reached nearly $3.9 billion, rising more than 210%. Meanwhile, customers generated 3.2 billion Agentic Work Units in the quarter, up 97% sequentially, pointing to stronger use of AI agents.
Higher adoption could support Salesforce in multiple ways. Bundles can increase spending from existing customers by adding AI features to current contracts. Deeper use of Agentforce, Slack and Data 360 can make Salesforce's platform more valuable and expand its recurring revenue base.
Still, AI growth has yet to materially change the company's overall growth rate. Second-quarter revenues rose 11% year over year to $11.35 billion, while management expects fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 11%-12%. Expanding AI bundles are a promising growth lever. If adoption remains strong, they could gradually accelerate Salesforce's recurring revenue growth.
Salesforce Rivals Intensify AI Bundle Competition
Salesforce is not the only enterprise software company using bundled AI products to increase customer spending. Its major competitors, Microsoft Corporation MSFT and Oracle Corporation ORCL, are also focusing on a similar approach.
Microsoft is expanding Microsoft 365 Copilot across its software ecosystem. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Microsoft 365 Copilot surpassed 30 million paid seats, with net seat additions more than doubling sequentially and the number of customers deploying above 50,000 seats growing more than sevenfold year over year. Microsoft's Dynamics 365 revenues also increased 13% year over year in the fourth quarter, showing continued demand for its business applications.
Oracle is taking a similar approach by adding AI capabilities to its cloud applications. The company is moving beyond traditional per-seat licensing to consumption-based token bundles. This approach lets enterprises pre-purchase agentic AI capacity in a predictable, scalable way across application tiers.
In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Oracle's Cloud Applications revenues reached $4.1 billion, up 10% year over year, while total cloud revenues jumped 47% to $9.9 billion. Oracle's AI-focused cloud strategy is also driving strong demand across its broader platform.
Salesforce's Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates
Salesforce shares have declined 10.6% year to date, while the Zacks Internet – Software industry has risen 9.2%.
From a valuation standpoint, CRM trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 14.65, significantly below the industry's average of 30.59.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Salesforce's fiscal 2027 earnings implies a year-over-year increase of approximately 33.5%, while estimates for fiscal 2028 indicate a 5% decline. Estimates for fiscal 2027 and 2028 earnings have been revised upward in the past 30 days.

Enterprise software continues to evolve as artificial intelligence changes how businesses operate. Choosing between Salesforce (CRM -0.84%) and CrowdStrike (CRWD +1.48%) depends on whether you prefer established stability or high-growth security.
Salesforce dominates the customer relationship management market, while CrowdStrike is a leader in cloud-native cybersecurity. Both companies are integrating advanced artificial intelligence to defend their market share. This comparison examines their financial health, growth trajectories, and current risks to help you decide which stock is the better addition to your long-term portfolio in 2026.
Salesforce sells software that helps companies manage every interaction they have with a customer using its unified Agentforce and Customer 360 platform. The company serves global clients of all sizes across the Americas, Europe, and Asia Pacific in the broader tech stocks landscape. In its latest annual report, Salesforce noted that no single customer accounted for more than 10% of its total revenue.
In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $41.5 billion, representing growth of roughly 9.6% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net income of approximately $7.5 billion during this period, resulting in a net margin of close to 18%. This net margin, which measures the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses are paid, has trended upward over the last three years.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.3x, which measures total debt against shareholder equity to show reliance on borrowing. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, is nearly 0.8x, and the company generated free cash flow of approximately $14.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
CrowdStrike provides cloud-native protection through its Falcon platform to stop digital breaches across corporate endpoints, cloud workloads, and identity systems. The company primarily uses a subscription model and serves over 23,000 customers globally across diverse environments. However, it continues to work through attrition and deferred purchases following a high-profile system configuration incident that occurred in 2024.
In FY 2026, revenue reached close to $4.8 billion, marking a growth rate of approximately 21.7% over the previous year. Despite the rising sales, the company reported a net loss of nearly $162.5 million and a negative net margin of roughly 3.4%.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x. The current ratio, which shows how easily a company can pay its upcoming bills, is roughly 1.8x, and the company generated free cash flow of close to $1.3 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 68% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Salesforce faces persistent risks from cyberattacks and potential unauthorized access to customer data, which could lead to significant legal liability. The rapid integration of generative AI introduces risks related to accuracy and evolving global regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act. Additionally, intense competition and the shift toward consumption-based pricing models create revenue forecasting uncertainty and pricing pressure while the company integrates its Informatica acquisition.
CrowdStrike continues to face adverse effects from its July 2024 system failure, which resulted in significant litigation and ongoing damage to customer relations. It operates in a fragmented market against massive competitors like Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%), and any perceived failure in its platform efficacy can cause immediate harm to brand trust. CrowdStrike also relies heavily on Amazon (AMZN +1.32%) for cloud infrastructure, meaning disruptions at that provider could negatively impact operations.
Salesforce looks cheaper based on its Forward P/E and P/S ratio. These compare share price to future earnings estimates and sales over the past twelve months.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with CrowdStrike, and after its most recent quarter, the results speak for themselves. The CEO called it the best quarter in the company's history. Net new annual recurring revenue hit a record, growing more than 50% year over year. Revenue grew at its fastest year-over-year pace in recent quarters, reaching 26% growth and beating estimates. And the company raised its full-year outlook substantially and generated record free cash flow. This is a business firing on every cylinder.
Salesforce deserves credit for its own strong execution. Agentforce has closed thousands of paid deals since launch, the AI and data cloud business more than doubled year over year, and the company is on track for a record year of operating cash flow. For investors who value predictable, recurring revenue and expanding margins, it is a solid long-term hold.
But CrowdStrike is growing faster, with an addressable market that keeps expanding as AI adoption creates new security challenges enterprises cannot ignore. If you're a patient investor like me, that kind of momentum is worth owning for the long haul.
